sec.title: Background
sec.p: Microbial lung infections may promote development of lung cancer through overlapping molecular mechanisms. This analysis aimed to identify a co-regulated peripheral blood gene signature in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and microbial lung infections.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A total of 403 peripheral blood transcriptomic profiles from five GEO test datasets—two LUAD (GSE39345, GSE103527) and three infection-related (GSE40012, GSE65682, GSE103119)—were analyzed using the limma package. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were defined by|log2FC| >1 and p < 0.05. Two additional GEO datasets (GSE42826 and GSE42830), comprising 30 blood samples (16 LUAD, 14 lung infection), served as validation sets. Shared DEGs were subjected to KEGG and GO enrichment analyses. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed in Cytoscape, and the top 10 hub genes were identified. Expression data of hub genes were compared between validation LUAD and lung infection samples using the Mann–Whitney U test, followed by linear regression and Pearson correlation to confirm co-regulation. Immune cell infiltration was assessed using xCell deconvolution algorithm.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Ninety-three significant DEGs were shared between LUAD and infection datasets, including 40 upregulated and 53 downregulated genes. Eight hub genes showed consistent differential expression in both LUAD and lung infection: BCL6, CD163, S100A12 (upregulated); and FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22, RPS4X (downregulated), of which BCL6, S100A12, FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22 and RPS4X were significantly co-regulated (R2 >0.8, p < 0.001) and correlated (p < 0.05). Immune profiling revealed that upregulated genes were associated with immunosuppressive cells such as Tregs and M2 macrophages, while downregulated genes were positively correlated with antitumor immune cell infiltration including CD8+ T cells and M1 macrophages. Consistent immune, stroma and microenvironment scores were observed between LUAD and lung infection.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This analysis identified a blood-based 7-gene signature shared between LUAD and microbial lung infections, associated with immunosuppressive microenvironment features, suggesting a potential link between infection-driven inflammation and tumor-promoting immune modulation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Globally considered as the leading cause of cancer-related death, lung cancer is a neoplastic growth originating from epithelial cells of the respiratory tract and is commonly classified into small cell lung cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the latter of which includes several important subtypes such as lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) [1]. From 2001 to 2019, more than 4,000,000 patients in the US were diagnosed with lung cancer [2], while in 2020, over 2,200,000 new cases of lung cancer were reported worldwide [3]. According to a 2023 meta-analysis of 32 studies, the overall mortality of lung cancer is estimated to range from 6 to 16% in different settings [4]. However, in the case of metastatic lung cancer, the statistics are far less favorable, with a meta-analysis of 70 phase III clinical trials suggesting an overall survival rate of 18.6% [5].

Microbial lung infections, such as bacterial pneumonias, have been recognized for complicating the process of treatment in lung cancer patients. It is well-established that incidence rates of such infections are generally higher in patients with lung cancer due to immunocompromised state as a result of chemotherapy [6]. For example, a recent investigation on 93 patients with advanced lung cancer and pneumonia identified Gram-negative bacteria as the major cause of infection that were present in 47.46% of patients receiving chemotherapy, and 61.77% of patients receiving targeted therapy [7]. Moreover, a retrospective cohort study involving 211 NSCLC patients reported 65 cases of infection, of which 71% were lung infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Hemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), among others [8]. Similarly, follow-up of 243 stage III/IV NSCLC patients revealed at least one type of infection in 147 patients (60.5%), of whom 43.2% had lung infections caused by bacterial strains in the majority of instances [9]. Other studies have also confirmed the considerably high proportions of microbial lung infections among all types of infections in lung cancer patients, with rates approaching 70% in certain reports [10].

Although lung cancer is known to predispose patients to lung infections, there is evidence suggesting that lung infections may increase the risk of developing lung cancer later in life. Epidemiological studies have consistently demonstrated this bidirectional relationship [11, 12]. For instance, hospitalization for pneumonia has been linked to a significantly elevated 1-year incidence of lung cancer compared to controls (2.1% vs. 0.1%), with heightened risk persisting for up to six years post-infection [11, 12]. A nationwide cohort study further revealed that patients with pneumococcal pneumonia had a 3.25-fold higher incidence rate of lung cancer than age- and sex-matched controls, even after adjusting for confounding factors [13]. Similarly, serological evidence indicates that chronic infection with Chlamydia pneumoniae is associated with a threefold increased risk of lung carcinoma, as indicated by elevated immunoglobulin A (IgA) and IgG antibody levels in cancer patients compared to healthy controls [14], with IgA being significantly associated with lymph node metastasis in lung cancer [15]. These findings suggest that microbial exposures may not merely coincide with lung cancer but could actively contribute to its development. A recent study of 334 LUAD patients identified marked differences in distribution of CD3+ and CD4+ T cells in LUAD patients with and without bacterial lung infections. Additionally, mechanistic insights from experimental models support this hypothesis. Streptococcus pneumoniae (SP), a common cause of bacterial pneumonia, has been shown to directly interact with lung epithelial cells via binding of pneumococcal surface protein C (PspC) to platelet-activating factor receptor (PAFR). This interaction activates pro-oncogenic pathways, including PI3K/AKT and NF-κB signaling, which drive cell proliferation, inflammation, and tumor growth in vivo [16]. The present evidence implies that recurrent or chronic lung infections might share pathogenic mechanisms with lung cancer, particularly through inflammation-driven molecular pathways and microbial-host interactions [17]. Co-regulated genes involved in immune evasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, or inflammation—such as those mediating PAFR expression or NF-κB activation—could serve as convergent nodes between the two conditions [16].

This bioinformatic analysis aims to address the underexplored hypothesis that lung cancer and microbial lung infections might share dysregulated molecular pathways, particularly within immune and inflammatory networks. Leveraging bioinformatics, we aimed to (1) identify genes with consistent expression patterns across these two lung diseases by analyzing Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets encompassing peripheral blood samples from patients with lung cancer and microbial lung infections, and (2) validate our findings using independent validation datasets including peripheral blood samples from patients with lung cancer and microbial lung infections. By integrating multi-disease transcriptomic data, this work pioneers a genome-wide approach to uncover overlapping genes and pathways that may inform dual-targeting strategies. The schematic design of study pipeline is presented in Fig. 1.

caption.p: Comprehensive bioinformatic analysis framework. Schematic representation of the integrated bioinformatic analysis workflow. The framework encompasses three parallel analytical pipelines—microbial lung infection, lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), and validation—which converge into a unified analytical pipeline. This consolidated framework facilitates sequential analyses including gene expression validation, functional enrichment analysis, protein–protein interaction network construction, assessment of gene co-regulation patterns, identification of shared gene signatures, and immune infiltration analysis

sec.title: Dataset selection
sec.p: Test datasets included GSE40012 [18], GSE65682 [19] and GSE103119 [20] for microbial lung infections, and GSE39345 [21] and GSE103527 [22] for LUAD, all containing peripheral blood samples. Validation datasets included GSE42826 and GSE42830 [23], comprised of peripheral blood samples from patients with lung cancer or lung infection from the same cohort. The characteristics of the datasets, including sample sizes, platforms, and patient demographics, are summarized in Table 1.

sec.title: Test dataset analysis
sec.p: Analysis of the test datasets was performed using the GEO2R tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/geo2r/) provided by NCBI, which leverages the Limma package (v3.52.4) in R. Patient samples were designated as cases and samples from healthy controls (without lung cancer or pneumonia) as controls. Background correction and force-normalization were applied consistently across all datasets. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using stringent criteria of|log2FC| >1 and adjusted P-value < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) correction for multiple testing. DEGs were pooled into a comprehensive DEG repository containing significantly up and downregulated genes shared between lung cancer and lung infection. Identification of shared DEGs was performed using VennPainter v1.2.0 [24], and verified using the UpSetR package (v1.4.0) to visualize intersections.

sec.title: Validation dataset analysis
sec.p: Validation datasets were analyzed using identical processing steps in GEO2R (Limma package) with slightly relaxed significance criteria (|log2FC| >0.58 and adjusted P-value < 0.05) after Benjamini-Hochberg correction, as samples originated from the same cohort, increasing sensitivity for detecting consistent signals across datasets. Significantly up and downregulated DEGs from validation datasets were used to generate a shared validation DEG pool, which was systematically compared against the test DEG pool to identify consistently dysregulated genes. Validated genes were required to show concordant direction of expression change in both test and validation datasets.

sec.title: Functional enrichment analysis
sec.p: Validated genes were analyzed for functional enrichment using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms via the clusterProfiler (v4.6.2), org.Hs.eg.db (v3.16.0), enrichplot (v1.11.1), and ggplot2 (v3.5.2) packages in R (v4.2). Enrichment was assessed using a significance threshold of p < 0.05 and q < 0.05. Significantly enriched pathways and GO terms were determined based on adjusted p-values and gene ratios, and were visualized according to gene count.

sec.title: Protein–protein interaction network analysis
sec.p: Protein–protein interaction (PPI) data were retrieved from STRING 12.0 (https://string-db.org/) with a minimum required interaction score of 0.7 (high confidence) to minimize false positives. The PPI network was constructed and visualized using Cytoscape v3.10.2. The CytoHubba plugin v0.1 was employed to identify hub genes using multiple centrality algorithms: maximal clique centrality (MCC), degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality. Consensus ranking from all four methods was used to identify the top 10 hub genes, which were color-coded based on rank in the network.

sec.title: Comparative analysis of hub gene expression
sec.p: Expression data for the top 10 hub genes were extracted from validation datasets (GSE42826 and GSE42830) comprising 30 peripheral blood samples (16 lung cancer, 14 pneumonia), all analyzed on the Illumina HumanHT-12 V4.0 expression platform. Expression values were quantile normalized using the preprocessCore package (v1.58.0) from Bioconductor in R. Comparative analysis between lung cancer and pneumonia samples was performed using both parametric (independent t-test) and non-parametric (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) approaches after assessing normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test. Genes showing significantly different expression (adjusted p < 0.05) between pathologies were excluded from further analysis.

sec.title: Hub gene Co-regulation and correlation analysis
sec.p: Hub genes without significant differences between pathologies were used to construct a linear regression model in Jamovi v2.3.28, an R-interface statistical software [25]. Co-regulation was assessed based adjusted R2 > 0.08 and p < 0.05, which was calculated using the F-test. A correlation matrix was constructed for co-regulated hub genes using the Pearson method, with correlations considered significant at p < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Ultimately, genes with confirmed co-regulation and significant correlation were defined as a shared gene signature.

sec.title: Immune cell infiltration analysis
sec.p: Immune cell infiltration analysis was performed using xCell deconvolution algorithm (https://xcell.ucsf.edu/) with 64 immune and stromal cell types. Correlation coefficients and adjusted p-values for each immune cell per gene were extracted and used to construct a correlation heatmap using the pheatmap package (v1.0.12) in R with hierarchical clustering (method="complete”, distance="euclidean”). Additionally, immune, stromal, and microenvironment scores were visualized in heatmap format with samples clustered based on patient group (lung cancer or lung infection).

sec.title: Analysis of test and validation datasets
sec.p: Results of the test dataset analysis are presented in Fig. 2, with comprehensive details available in Supplementary File S1 (encompassing GSE39345, GSE40012, GSE65652, GSE103119, and GSE103527 on separate sheets). Boxplot visualizations of normalized gene expression in selected samples from all datasets are presented in Supplementary Figs. S1–S5. Analysis of lung cancer datasets yielded 2924 DEGs, comprising 1607 upregulated and 1317 downregulated genes, which collectively formed the lung cancer test DEG pool. Comparative analysis of lung infection datasets identified 2057 DEGs (919 upregulated and 1138 downregulated), which were aggregated to establish the lung infection test DEG pool. The complete compilation of test DEG pools is provided in Supplementary File S1 (Test DEG Pool sheet). Table 2 summarizes the logFC values and adjusted P values for the top ten DEGs identified in each test dataset.

sec.p: Each validation dataset underwent a two-tiered analytical approach, wherein peripheral blood samples from lung cancer and lung infection subjects were simultaneously compared against control samples to generate two distinct validation DEG pools, designated as batch 1 and batch 2 (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Differential Expression Analysis of Validation Datasets. Volcano plots and Venn diagrams highlighting significant DEGs (|logFC| >0.58, p < 0.05) used to generate validation DEG pools from A GSE42826 and B GSE42830. Lung cancer and pneumonia samples from both datasets were analyzed and compared to controls in parallel

sec.p: Analysis of the GSE42826 dataset identified 2080 DEGs, with 780 genes exhibiting shared expression patterns between lung cancer and lung infection samples, constituting validation batch (1) similarly, analysis of the GSE42830 dataset yielded 2280 DEGs, of which 875 demonstrated common expression patterns across both pathologies, forming validation batch (2) upon integration of both validation batches, 501 DEGs were identified as consistently present across both validation pools. A comprehensive inventory of genes comprising the validation DEG pool is documented in Supplementary File S1 (Validation DEG Pool sheet).

Comparative analysis was conducted between the test DEG pools (lung cancer and lung infection) and validation pools to authenticate shared DEGs across datasets. This rigorous cross-validation process identified 93 consistently differentially expressed genes, comprising 40 upregulated and 53 downregulated genes. Figure 4 presents a comprehensive heatmap visualization of all validated differentially expressed genes, illustrating their expression patterns across the analyzed samples.

caption.p: Heatmap of validated DEGs. The heatmap illustrates 93 validated DEGs—53 downregulated and 40 upregulated—across the validation datasets and patient groups. Color intensity reflects the log fold-change (logFC), with red denoting upregulation (positive logFC) and blue denoting downregulation (negative logFC). Within each patient group, logFC represents the expression fold-change relative to normal controls

sec.title: Functional enrichment analyses
sec.p: The functional enrichment analysis results are presented in Fig. 5. The KEGG pathway analysis revealed significant enrichment in several immune-related pathways, most notably neutrophil degranulation, signaling by interleukins, and IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, indicating potential immunological associations.

caption.p: Functional enrichment analyses. Top enriched KEGG pathways (A), and GO biological process (B), cellular component (C) and molecular function (D) terms. Circle size and color indicate the number of genes mapped to each pathway and P value, respectively

sec.p: The Gene Ontology enrichment analysis, also illustrated in Fig. 5, further supported these immunological implications. The analysis identified enrichment in multiple categories:

list-item.p: Biological process: Predominant terms included lymphocyte differentiation, mononuclear cell differentiation, and T cell differentiation (p ≤ 0.003).
Cellular component: Tertiary granule and secretory/tertiary granule membrane demonstrated high enrichment (p ≤ 0.003).
Molecular function: DNA binding transcription repressor activity, β-catenin binding, and transcription corepressor binding were significantly enriched (p ≤ 0.003).

sec.title: PPI network analysis
sec.p: A protein–protein interaction network was constructed using the 93 validated genes, as depicted in Fig. 6. The resulting interaction network comprises 33 nodes and 65 edges (p < 0.05). Hub genes were identified based on MCC and degree score calculations. The analysis revealed ten predominant hub genes: MMP9, FLT3LG, RPL14, RPS4X, RPL22, RPL13, S100A12, CD163, IL1RN, and BCL6. The comprehensive data underlying the protein–protein interaction network is available in Supplementary File S1 (PPI sheet). The complete PPI network consisting of 90 nodes and 83 edges is visualized in Supplementary Fig. S6.

caption.p: Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network of validated DEGs. The PPI network highlights the top 10 hub genes, ranked by Maximal Clique Centrality (MCC) and color-coded by rank (red, orange, yellow)

sec.p: Table 3 provides a comprehensive summary of the logFC values for these hub genes across both test and validation datasets, quantifying their differential expression patterns.

caption.p: Quantitative summary of the expression of hub genes shared between lung infection and lung cancer in test and validation datasets

sec.title: Comparative analysis of hub gene expression in validation datasets
sec.p: Expression values of the ten identified hub genes from the protein–protein interaction network were extracted from peripheral blood samples in the validation datasets, comprising lung cancer (N = 16) and lung infection (N = 14) samples. These values underwent normalization prior to comparative analysis (Fig. 7). The distribution patterns of hub genes demonstrated substantial consistency across both disease states.

caption.p: Normalization and expression profiling of hub genes. Peripheral blood expression data from lung cancer and lung infection patients (validation datasets) shown A before and B after quantile normalization. Scatterplots display hub gene expression in lung cancer versus lung infection, color-coded by C gene identity and D regulation pattern

sec.p: To validate concordant expression profiles between lung cancer and lung infection, normalized expression levels of these hub genes were statistically compared between the two pathologies (Fig. 8). This analysis revealed significant differential expression for IL1RN (p = 0.009) and MMP9 (p = 0.015) between lung cancer and lung infection samples, necessitating their exclusion from further consideration. The remaining eight genes—BCL6, CD163, S100A12, FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22, and RPS4X—exhibited no statistically significant differences between the pathologies, confirming comparable expression levels across these distinct pulmonary conditions.

caption.p: Boxplots of normalized hub gene expression. Expression levels of A BCL6, B FLT3LG, C CD163, D RPL13, E IL1RN, F RPL14, G MMP9, H RPL22, I S100A12, and J RPS4X are compared between lung cancer and lung infection samples from validation datasets

sec.title: Analysis of hub gene co-regulation and correlation
sec.p: The eight shared hub genes exhibiting insignificant differential expression between lung cancer and lung infection—comprising three upregulated (BCL6, CD163, S100A12) and five downregulated (FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22, RPS4X) genes—underwent linear regression analysis to evaluate expression pattern consistency across both pathologies. As illustrated in Fig. 9, collective analysis of these genes as a signature demonstrated consistent expression patterns in both lung cancer and lung infection, with robust coefficient of determination values (R2 >0.8) and high statistical significance (p < 0.01).

caption.p: Linear regression models for hub gene expression. Regression lines depict expression trends in lung cancer versus lung infection for A upregulated hub genes (BCL6, CD163, S100A12), B downregulated hub genes (FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22, RPS4X), and C all eight hub genes combined

sec.p: To assess inter-gene relationships among the co-regulated hub genes, correlation analysis was performed, with results visualized in the heatmap presented in Fig. 10. The analysis revealed that CD163 did not demonstrate significant correlation with the remaining seven genes. Significant positive correlations were observed among upregulated genes (BCL6 and S100A12) and among downregulated genes (FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22, and RPS4X). Furthermore, significant negative correlations were identified between upregulated and downregulated genes, confirming that these seven genes constitute a coherent gene signature associated with both lung cancer and lung infection.

caption.p: Correlation matrix of genes in the proposed gene signature. Positive correlations are shown in blue and negative correlations in red. Statistical significance is indicated by asterisks (p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001)

sec.title: Immune cell infiltration analysis
sec.p: To assess potential pro-oncogenic activity of the proposed gene signature, immune cell infiltration analysis was conducted, with results presented in Fig. 11A. FLT3LG exhibited the strongest correlations with specific immune cell populations, including positive associations with CD8 + T cells, follicular helper T cells, activated natural killer (NK) cells, and M1 macrophages, alongside negative associations with T regulatory cells and M2 macrophages. These correlations potentially indicate pro-immunosuppressive effects in both lung cancer and lung infection contexts, particularly considering FLT3LG’s significant downregulation in these conditions. Similar pro-immunosuppressive correlation patterns were also evident for BCL6, S100A12, RPL13, RPL14, and RPL22, albeit with lower degree of correlation compared to FLT3LG. It should be noted that the peripheral blood origin of the analyzed samples may account for the relatively modest correlation strengths observed, as immune cell infiltration analyses typically demonstrate stronger transcriptional associations in tumor tissue samples.

caption.p: Immune cell infiltration analysis. A Heatmap showing correlations between gene signature expression and immune cell lineage infiltration. Significant positive correlations appear in red, negative in blue (p < 0.05); nonsignificant correlations are shown as grey blanks. B Heatmap of xCell-derived global scores (stroma, immune, microenvironment), clustered by patient group

sec.p: Further analysis of stroma score, immune score, and microenvironment score across samples (categorized by disease type) is visualized in the heatmap (Fig. 11B). This analysis revealed substantial consistency between disease groups, with only three lung cancer samples exhibiting notably divergent scoring patterns.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our comparative analysis of transcriptome data from patients with microbial lung infections and lung cancer revealed that BCL6 is significantly upregulated in both pathologies, suggesting a shared mechanism in disease progression, consistent with its known oncogenic role in KRAS-driven lung cancer via the MAPK/ERK/ELK1 pathway [26]. In both conditions, BCL6 creates an immunosuppressive microenvironment by negatively associating with CD8+ T cells and M1 macrophages while positively correlating with Tregs, M2 macrophages, and neutrophils. BCL6 suppresses M1 polarization and promotes M2 skewing through JNK inhibition [27], while sustaining neutrophil survival at inflammation sites [28]. This parallels BCL6’s role in viral respiratory infections, where it correlates with disease severity and interferon signaling [29]. Chronic BCL6 activation may create conditions favoring tumor development through sustained immunosuppression and inflammation, as evidenced by its stabilization in advanced NSCLC [30]. BCL6 inhibition represents a potential therapeutic strategy targeting both neoplastic and inflammatory pathways [26].

S100A12, a calcium-binding damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) protein, is significantly upregulated in both lung infection and lung cancer, suggesting a shared immunomodulatory role. Our immune infiltration analysis shows S100A12 correlates negatively with anti-tumorigenic immune cells (Th1/Th2 cells, NK cells, M1 macrophages) while positively associating with immunosuppressive M2 macrophages. This aligns with S100A12’s known links to inflammation and immune dysregulation in severe infections, including its association with monocyte/macrophage signatures in carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) infection [31] and correlation with severity and mortality in community-acquired pneumonia [32]. While S100A12 exhibits antimicrobial activity against S. pneumoniae via membrane disruption and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation [33], it also mediates systemic immune suppression by expanding granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs), impairing T-cell function, and increasing secondary infection risk [34]. In lung cancer contexts, S100A12 has been detected in benign pulmonary nodules [35] and may promote inflammation through RAGE-dependent chemotaxis of tumor-associated myeloid cells [36]. S100A12’s interaction with toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/RAGE pathways [36] could synergize with its effects on MDSCs/macrophage polarization [33, 35], potentially creating a feedback loop that perpetuates chronic inflammation and immune exhaustion, representing a possible pathogenic link between unresolved infection and tumorigenesis.

In blood transcriptome analyses of microbial lung infection and lung cancer patients, significant FLT3LG downregulation was observed in both conditions, with distinctive immune infiltration patterns suggesting immunoregulatory functions. FLT3LG, which regulates dendritic cell (DC) differentiation and NK cell-mediated antitumor immunity [37, 38], negatively correlated with immunosuppressive cell types (Tregs, Th2 cells, M2 macrophages, neutrophils) while positively associating with CD8 + T cells, M1 macrophages, activated NK cells, and mature DCs. This is in agreement with evidence linking FLT3LG to favorable prognosis in lymphomas through enhanced T-cell infiltration [39]. In lung cancer, FLT3LG downregulation may impair DC-mediated antigen cross-presentation and reduce NK cell-driven chemokine production essential for cDC1 maturation and adaptive immunity [37, 40]. In bacterial pneumonia, reduced FLT3LG could compromise host defense by limiting DC expansion, consistent with its role as a biomarker of immune responsiveness in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) [41]. The shared signatures between conditions suggest common immunopathogenic mechanisms where FLT3LG suppression favors immunosuppressive myeloid populations while reducing cytotoxic and antigen-presenting cell activity. The simultaneous positive association with M1 macrophages and negative correlation with regulatory T cells reflects The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) findings in lung cancer, where FLT3LG expression correlated with prolonged survival despite increased T-cell exhaustion markers [38].

Our analysis revealed significant RPL14 downregulation in blood transcriptomes, with distinctive immune infiltration patterns. The role of RPL14 in bacterial lung infections has rarely been explored. While severe COVID-19 studies report RPL14 upregulation in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) correlating with disease severity and dysregulated protein synthesis [42], our microbial lung infection findings suggest context-dependent immune modulation roles, possibly reflecting pathogen-specific responses as ribosomal proteins increasingly feature in pathogen-sensing and translational control during infections [42]. In lung cancer, RPL14 maps to chromosome 3p21.3, a frequently deleted tumor suppressor region; however, its blood sample downregulation independent of genomic deletion aligns with transcriptional loss observed in squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) [43]. Mechanistically, RPL14 negatively correlates with Th1 cells, M2 macrophages, and activated DCs, suggesting suppression of pro-inflammatory or anti-tumor immunity. Conversely, its positive association with CD8+ T cells, follicular helper T cells, γδ T cells, and monocyte-derived macrophages indicates a dual role in sustaining specific immune subsets that may combat infection or promote tumor immunosuppression [43]. Given its ribosomal function, RPL14 downregulation could impair immune cell translational capacity, altering activation states or differentiation trajectories as seen in ribosomopathies [43], suggesting potential immunological cross-talk between chronic lung infection and cancer through RPL14-mediated immune cell homeostasis dysregulation.

Our findings show RPL22 downregulation in both lung infection and lung cancer, indicating a mechanistic link between these conditions. This observation aligns with evidence from sepsis-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), where RPL22 downregulation associated with reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration and increased immunosuppressive Treg activity [44]. Here, RPL22 expression negatively correlated with Tregs but positively with CD8+ T cells, Th1 cells, and M1 macrophages, indicating RPL22’s conserved role in modulating anti-pathogen and anti-tumor immunity. In lung cancer, RPL22 loss has been linked to oncogenic processes through inhibition of casein kinase 2α (CK2α), which is associated with apoptosis evasion and unchecked proliferation [45]. CK2α activity also maintains Treg function and M2 macrophage polarization in the tumor microenvironment [45], suggesting RPL22 downregulation may promote both tumor growth and immune evasion through CK2α dysregulation. Beyond its ribosomal function, RPL22’s extraribosomal interactions, including p53-dependent T cell checkpoint activation [44]—could connect immunological deficits in both diseases. Chronic inflammation from unresolved pneumonia may sustain RPL22 suppression, potentially creating conditions favorable for malignant transformation by compromising both anti-microbial immunity and tumor surveillance. Despite limited evidence for RPL22 as a circulating biomarker in lung cancer [46], these findings highlight it as a potential link between infection-associated immune dysfunction and oncogenic pathways.

We also noted significant downregulation of RPS4X in blood samples from both lung infection and lung cancer patients, proposing a shared molecular perturbation. While existing literature primarily documents RPS4X dysregulation in viral infections like respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and severe actute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), where it contributes to immune dysfunction and viral manipulation of host translation [47, 48], our findings suggest its relevance may extend to bacterial infections through conserved translational regulation mechanisms. In lung cancer, RPS4X’s role is less characterized, though one study linked its tumor tissue overexpression to GTF2E2-mediated mTOR pathway activation promoting tumor growth [49]. The contrast between systemic downregulation and intratumoral upregulation suggests compartment-specific functions: reduced systemic RPS4X may reflect host response to infection or tumor-driven immune evasion, while intratumoral activity could support oncogenic processes via mTOR signaling. Immune infiltration analyses revealed RPS4X negatively correlates with immunosuppressive cells (Tregs, M2 macrophages) and positively with cytotoxic (NK cells, M1 macrophages) and helper T cells (CD8, Th2), suggesting a dual role in modulating immunity. These patterns align with evidence that ribosomal proteins influence immune cell polarization and cytokine production [47, 48], potentially connecting infection-induced inflammation with tumor microenvironment remodeling. This convergence may reflect shared pathogenic strategies exploiting ribosomal machinery to subvert immune surveillance or compensatory host mechanisms. The limited evidence in lung cancer highlights the need to explore how RPS4X regulation intersects with tumor-immune interactions, particularly given its association with mTOR signaling [49], which is critical to both cancer metabolic reprogramming and immune function.

Collectively, our proposed gene signature consisting of BCL6, S100A12, FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22 and RPS4X was associated with increased immunosuppressive and reduced anti-tumor immune activity, potentially suggesting a shared pathogenic axis linking microbial lung infections, including bacterial pneumonia, to lung cancer.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The present analysis has several limitations. First, the validation of the identified shared gene signature was conducted in silico using publicly available datasets (i.e., GSE42826 and GSE42830), and no experimental or clinical validation was performed. Second, while the inclusion of peripheral blood samples from both lung adenocarcinoma and microbial lung infections aimed to enhance cross-condition consistency, it is important to note that blood-based gene expression profiles may vary between cancer-related and infection-related systemic responses, potentially influencing the comparability of DEGs. Third, although the number of test samples was relatively high (N = 403), the validation datasets were modest in size, particularly for lung infection (N = 14) and lung cancer (N = 16), which may affect the robustness of statistical validation. Additionally, due to the use of peripheral blood transcriptomic data and the limited number of genes in the final panel (seven genes), immune cell infiltration analysis was performed using the xCell algorithm on a subset of 64 samples, as CIBERSORTx was not optimal for such input. Finally, although the hub genes showed strong co-regulation and immune relevance, the mechanistic link between infection-driven immune modulation and tumorigenesis remains to be experimentally clarified.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our comparative transcriptome analysis reveals convergent molecular and immune regulatory mechanisms in microbial lung infections and lung cancer, centered on the dysregulation of BCL6, S100A12, FLT3LG, RPL13, RPL14, RPL22, and RPS4X. These genes influence immune cell composition and function, with consistent patterns indicating the development of an immunosuppressive microenvironment across both conditions. The shared activation of immune evasion pathways—including cytotoxic response suppression and enrichment of regulatory and myeloid-derived suppressor cells—suggests that chronic inflammation in infection may predispose to or co-evolve with tumorigenesis. Strengthening the reliability of these findings, our bioinformatic results were validated using two additional independent peripheral blood datasets from patients with lung cancer and pneumonia. Furthermore, co-regulation of the candidate genes was confirmed through regression and correlation analyses, providing robust statistical support. However, the study’s reliance on publicly available GEO datasets without experimental validation limits causal interpretation. While functional studies are necessary to establish mechanistic links, these findings offer compelling evidence that shared immune regulatory pathways between infection and cancer may serve as potential biomarkers or therapeutic targets, warranting further investigation.
